title: Stoic at work
hook: duties, roles, and control at work

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Stoic evening: Sextius's questions and Seneca's pardon. Your line was three questions.

Sunday night, around eight. The feeling arrives on schedule: the project that's behind, the manager who's hard to read, the rumor about layoffs, the colleague who takes credit. Some of it is real work. Some of it is weather. All of it lands in the same knot in your stomach. The Stoics didn't have open-plan offices. But many of Epictetus's students were young men headed for posts in public life, and Marcus wrote his notebook while hearing cases and running campaigns. They had a lot to say about doing work without letting it own you.
screen: `SUNDAY NIGHT, EIGHT O'CLOCK.` → `REAL WORK, AND WEATHER.` → `ONE KNOT IN THE STOMACH.`

segments.voice: First, the split. The Handbook opens with it: some things are up to us, and some are not. At work, that sorts quickly. Up to you: how carefully you do the task, how honestly you speak, how you treat the people around you, whether you ask for help. Not up to you: the budget, the reorganization, whether your manager likes your idea, the economy. Second, roles. You met this idea with Cicero a month ago; Epictetus puts it in one line: our duties are measured by our relationships. You're a colleague, so act as a good colleague. You're someone's manager, or someone's report: ask what that role asks of you, today, at this desk. Third, the Stoic word. Kathēkon: an appropriate action, the fitting thing for someone in your place to do. It isn't heroic. It's the email answered clearly, the meeting attended fully, the mistake owned up to. Fourth, together. A lot of work worry comes from mixing the two columns: carrying the layoff rumor as if it were your task, or treating your own sloppy report as if it were fate. Sort them, and the knot loosens a little. The first column gets your full effort. The second gets your attention, maybe your preparation, but not your sleep. Marcus reminded himself more than once to do the thing in front of him with simple dignity, as if it were the last thing he would ever do.
screen: `UP TO ME, NOT UP TO ME.` · `DUTIES MEASURED BY ROLES.` · `KATHĒKON: THE FITTING THING.` · `TWO COLUMNS, ONE KNOT LOOSENED.` · then, large: `MY PART AT WORK.`

segments.voice: Bring one worry from work, school, volunteering or caregiving to mind, and picture a page with two columns. On the left, up to me: what you can actually do; on the right, not up to me: what you can't control, and let those stay there. Look at the left column only, and let one thing from it stand out.
Kathēkon, the Stoic word for the fitting action: doing your role's appropriate part fully, and leaving what isn't up to you in its own column. Today's word.
Your line: my part at work. The fitting thing is usually a small one. Day six hundred seventy-seven.

howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners sort work worries into what is and isn't up to them, then give full effort to their own part and the duties of their role.

chat.says: Layoff rumors are everywhere. What would a Stoic actually do about it?
options: Sort it: rumors aren't up to me, so my best effort goes to the work that is.
Ignore it completely, since a Stoic shouldn't care what happens at work.
Worry hard now, so that the bad news won't hurt as much if it comes.
chat.meaning: The Handbook's split: some things are up to us, some aren't. The fitting action gets full effort; the rumor gets attention, not your sleep.

Kathēkon.meaning: Stoic word: the fitting, appropriate action

Handbook.meaning: Epictetus's short manual of Stoic teaching

notes: Enchiridion 1 (up to us / not), 30 (duties measured by relations) paraphrased. Confirm.
